text:
1.1 Data generation and visualisation
The single-layer perceptron is the simplest neural network, which takes a feature (input), weights it to form a weighted sum, and then passes this to an activation function. The result can then be used for binary classification or linear regression (without activation). It is an ideal starting point for understanding the basic mechanics of neural networks, which we will use to build the foundations of the course.
Objective of this chapter:
How does a neuron process inputs?
How do weights influence the decision?
What does ‘linearly separable’ mean?
Why does the perceptron fail with some problems, such as XOR?
To begin with, we first create two-dimensional data points based on the logical gates AND / OR. This enables a clear visual representation and shows us immediately whether the data is linearly separable.
Info: The perceptron developed by Rosenblatt in 1957 cannot solve linearly non-separable data such as the XOR problem. We take advantage of this property and generate linearly separable and non-separable data sets to reveal the functioning and limitations of the model.
Creating features and labels

title: 1  Perceptron
text:
1.2 Das Perzeptron als Modell
Das Perzeptron verarbeitet Eingaben in drei aufeinanderfolgenden Schritten:

1.2.1 1. Eingabe
Das Modell erhält einen Eingabevektor x, den Featurevektor.


1.2.2 2. Berechnung
Die Eingabe wird über die Gewichte w und den Bias-Parameter b linear transformiert. z nennen wir die gewichtete Summe:
\[z = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b\]


1.2.3 3. Ausgabe
Die gewichtete Summe z übergeben wir einer nichtlinearen Aktivierungsfunktion, beim Rosenblatt Perceptron klassisch die Step Function. Beim Perzeptron nennen wir das Ergebnis davon die Prediction des Modells:
\[\hat{y} = \text{step}(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{falls } z \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text{sonst} \end{cases}\]


1.2.4 Vollständiger Datenfluss
Der gesamte Prozess lässt sich wie folgt darstellen:
\[\mathbf{x} \longrightarrow \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b \longrightarrow \text{step}(z) \longrightarrow \hat{y}\]

title: 1  Perceptron
text:
1.3 Aktivierungsfunktion definieren
Neben der eben definierten Step Function, führen wir an dieser Stelle die Sigmoid Aktivierungsfunktion ebenfalls ein, welchen wir mit einer modifizierten Lernregel später für das Perzeptron und den Multi Layer Perzeptron verwenden. Im deep learning gibt es eine Vielzahl von verschiedenen Aktivierungen, einige werden wir uns im Verlauf anschauen.
Eine visuelle Inspektion verrät uns auf Anhieb schon einige Eigenschaften, welche direkt sichbar sind, zusätzlich gibt es versteckte Eigenschaften, welche man nicht durch das scharfe sehen direkt erkennt. Für uns ist das im Moment irrelevant, da wir erstmal eine Intuition zum Workflow bilden wollen. Wir werden das im Kapitel Aktivierung und Featureraum der Beginnersektion näher beleuchten und später umfassend in der Intermidatesektion.
Sigmoid: \[ f(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} \]
Man erkennt auf Anhieb: - Wertebereich liegt in (0,1) - monoton steigend - für große |x| nähert sich der Wert 0 oder 1 an - stetig differenzierbar
Der Ausgabe der Sigmoid-Funktion kann eine Semantik mitgegeben werden. Für die Binärklassifikation bedeutet das: - \(\sigma(z) < 0.5\) → Klasse 0 - \(\sigma(z) >= 0.5\) → Klasse 1
Step Function:
Man erkennt auf Anhieb: - Werte können nur 0 oder 1 annehmen - x = 0 ist nicht definiert - selbst wenn differenzierbar, Steigung = 0 -> kein nutzbarer Gradient -> kein Informationsgehalt


Code
def step_function(x: np.ndarray):
  return np.where(x >= 0, 1, 0)

def sigmoid(x: np.ndarray):
  return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

def sigmoid_derivative(x: np.ndarray):
  ds = (np.exp(-x))/(1+np.exp(-x))**2
  return ds

x = np.linspace(-10, 10, 100)
fig4, ax4 = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))

ax4.plot(x, sigmoid(x), c="blue", label="Sigmoid")
ax4.plot(x, sigmoid_derivative(x), c="red", label="Sigmoid derivative")
ax4.plot(x[x < 0], step_function(x[x < 0]), c="orange", label="Step Function")
ax4.plot(x[x >= 0], step_function(x[x >= 0]), c="orange")

ax4.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax4.set_xlabel("x")
ax4.set_ylabel("f(x)")

title: 1  Perceptron
text:
1.4 Perzeptron-Klasse implementieren
Nun implementieren wir das Perzeptron als Klasse. Wir haben bereits die Architektur beleuchtet, nun widmen wir uns der Lernregel.

1.4.1 Klassische Perzeptron-Lernregel
Das Perzeptron lernt, indem es seine Gewichte nur dann anpasst, wenn es einen Fehler macht.
Für jedes Trainingsbeispiel wird die Prediction \(\hat{y}\) mit dem wahren Label \(y\) verglichen.
Daraus ergibt sich ein Fehlerterm:
\[
\delta = y - \hat{y}
\]

Wenn \(\delta = 0\):
Die Vorhersage ist korrekt → keine Anpassung.
Wenn \(\delta = 1\):
Das Perzeptron hat \(0\) vorhergesagt, obwohl \(1\) korrekt wäre →
Die Gewichte sollen in Richtung von \(\mathbf{x}\) verschoben werden.
Wenn \(\delta = -1\):
Das Perzeptron hat \(1\) vorhergesagt, obwohl \(0\) korrekt wäre →
Die Gewichte sollen von \(\mathbf{x}\) weg verschoben werden.

Die klassische Perzeptron-Lernregel lautet:
\[
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta \, \delta \, \mathbf{x}
\]
\[
b \leftarrow b + \eta \, \delta
\]
wobei \(\eta\) die Lernrate ist.

1.4.1.1 Intuition

Falsch klassifizierte positive Beispiele (\(y = 1\)) „ziehen” den Gewichtsvektor in ihre Richtung.
Falsch klassifizierte negative Beispiele (\(y = 0\)) „stoßen” den Gewichtsvektor von sich weg.
Korrekt klassifizierte Beispiele haben keinen Einfluss auf die Gewichte.

Auf diese Weise verschiebt das Perzeptron seine Entscheidungsgrenze so lange, bis alle Trainingspunkte (falls linear separierbar) korrekt klassifiziert werden.



Code
class Perzeptron:
    def __init__(self, input_size, activation_function):

        self.weight = rng.normal(size=(input_size,1))
        self.bias = 0.
        self.activation = activation_function

    def forward(self, X):
        """
        Berechnet die Ausgabe des Perzeptrons für ein Feauture X.

        Args:
            X: Eingabedaten, Shape (n_samples, n_features)
        Returns:
            Ausgabe des Perzeptrons nach Aktiverung, Shape (n_samples, 1)
        """
        z = X @ self.weight + self.bias
        a = self.activation(z)
        return a

    def train(self, X, y , lr=0.1, epochs=1000, error_prints=True):
        """
        Trains the perceptron using the perceptron (error-count) learning rule.

        Args:
            X (np.ndarray): Input data of shape (n_samples, n_features).
            y (np.ndarray): Target labels of shape (n_samples, 1) 
            lr (float): Learning rate
            epochs (int): Maximum number of training epochs.
            error_prints (bool) : Printing error rates -> set False for timelapse

        Returns:
            list[float]: List of error_rate per epoch
            list[float]: List of update_rate per epoch
        """
    
        error_history, update_history = [], []

        for epoch in range(epochs):
            fehler_count = 0
            for xi, yi in zip(X,y):
                xi = np.reshape(xi, (1,-1)) # (1, n_features)
                yi = np.reshape(yi, (-1,1)) # (1, 1) 
                #Forward pass 
                y_hat = self.forward(xi)

                #Calc delta
                delta = (yi - y_hat)
                delta = np.squeeze(delta)
                delta = float(delta)

                #Update weights and bias
                if delta != 0:
                    self.weight += lr * delta * xi.T
                    self.bias += lr * delta
                    fehler_count += 1

            update_rate = fehler_count/len(y)
            y_hat = self.forward(X)
            error_rate = float(np.mean(y != y_hat))
            error_history.append(error_rate)            
            update_history.append(update_rate)

            if error_prints:
                if epoch % 10 == 0:
                    print(f'Epoch {epoch}: Error Rate = {error_rate:.4f}')

            if error_rate == 0:
                print(f"Solution in Epoch {epoch}")
                return error_history, update_history
                
        return error_history, update_history

1.5 Das primäre Problem
Wir bauen im Laufe des Kurses viele verschiedene Architekturen von Scratch nach. Diese Architekturen werden immer komplexer, und wir werden nicht darum herumkommen, uns mit Bugs und noch schlimmer mit „hidden“ Fehlern zu beschäftigen, die bsw. durch falsche Shapes oder unerwartetes NumPy-Broadcasting entstehen. Deshalb mal ein beispiel wie ich die von Scratch implementierte Trainingsloop getestet habe.
Broadcasting kann uns das Leben zwar stark erleichtern und ist oft gut darin zu erraten, was wir meinen, zum Beispiel in einer Zeile wie z = X @ self.w + self.b. Aber genau das kann auch dazu führen, dass wir Fehler erst sehr spät entdecken, weil der Code zwar läuft, aber stillschweigend etwas anderes tut als gedacht.

        assert isinstance(error_rate, (float)), "error_rate must be float"
        assert isinstance(update_rate, (float)), "update_rate must float)"

text:
1.6 Das mathematische Modell
Das trainierte Perzeptron können wir und als Funktion ausgeben lassen. Das dient zur Verständnisbildung, denn neuronale Netze egal ob tief oder nicht sind nichts anderes als mathematische Modelle. Weil das Perzeptron so simpel ist kann man sich das ausgeben lassen, normalerweise untersucht man die gelernten gewichte und den bias. Aber das machen wir in einem späterem Kapitel.


Code
w_flat = model.weight.flatten()  
w1, w2 = w_flat
b = model.bias
print(f"f(x1,x2) = step({w1:.3f}*x1 + {w2:.3f}*x2 + {b:.3f})")


f(x1,x2) = step(0.142*x1 + 0.081*x2 + -0.200)



1.6.1 Entscheidungsgrenze visualisieren

2.5 5.Lossfunction
Wir können direkt erkennen, dass unsere zufällig generierte Funktion die Daten nicht gut abbildet. Um das zu quantifizieren, brauchen wir eine Verlustfunktion.
Für das Regressionsproblem, welches wir lösen wollen, halten wir es simpel mit dem Mean Squared Error. Wie man in der Summenschreibweise erkennt, gibt es bei unserem linearen Modell einen Kopplungsterm \(2 \cdot b \cdot w \cdot \sum(x)\). Durch das Zentrieren von \(x\) wird die Summe 0 und somit fällt der Term später weg. Bei unseren Daten mit Rauschen wird dieser kleiner und auch somit der Einfluss von \(w\) auf \(b\) in Bezug auf das MSE und vice versa.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\displaystyle
MSE &= \frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} error_i^2 \\[8pt]
    &= \frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2 \\[8pt]
    &= \frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} (b + w x_i - y_i)^2 \\[8pt]
    &= \frac{1}{n} \Bigg(
        \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} y_i^2
        - 2b \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} y_i
        - 2w \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i
        + b^2 n
        + {\color{red}{2bw \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i}}
        + w^2 \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2
      \Bigg)
\end{aligned}
\]
Als nächstes setzen wir den Error über den Trainingsdatensatz in unsere Funktion ein, hier über error = (yhat-y).

class Calculator():
  def __init__(self, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, start_axis=0, stop_axis=4):
    try:
      assert x.size == y.size, "Shape missmatch, can cause Problems later"
    except AssertionError as error:
      print(error)
    self.x = x
    self.y = y
    #Terms
    self.Syy = np.sum(y**2)
    self.Sxy = np.sum(y * x)
    self.Sxx = np.sum(x**2)
    self.Sx = np.sum(x)
    self.Sy = np.sum(y)
    self.n = len(y)

    #axis
    self.w_axis : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.b_axis : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.w_mesh : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.b_mesh : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.set_mesh(start_axis,stop_axis)

  def mse(self, w = None, b = None, is_mesh=False):
    if w is not None and b is not None:
      w = np.asarray(w)
      b = np.asarray(b)
    elif (w is None) != (b is None):
      raise ValueError("w or b value missing")
    else:
      if not is_mesh:
          w = self.w_axis
          b = self.b_axis
      else:
        w = self.w_mesh
        b = self.b_mesh

    term = (self.Syy - 2*w*self.Sxy - 2*b*self.Sy + w**2 * self.Sxx
            + 2*w*b*self.Sx + self.n*(b**2) )
    mse = term/self.n
    return mse


  def grad_b(self,w,b):
    term = (- 2*self.Sy
            + 2*w*self.Sx + 2*self.n*(b))
    dmse_db = term/self.n
    return dmse_db

  def grad_w(self,w,b):
    term = (- 2*self.Sxy + 2 * w * self.Sxx
            + 2*b*self.Sx )
    dmse_dw = term/self.n
    return dmse_dw

  def set_mesh(self,start,stop, n=1):
    if n == 1:
      n = self.n
    self.w_axis = np.linspace(start,stop,n)
    self.b_axis = np.linspace(start,stop,n)
    self.w_mesh, self.b_mesh = np.meshgrid(self.w_axis,self.b_axis)

text:
2.6 6. Partielle Ableitungen und Gradient Descent in 1D
Um zu verstehen, wie sich die Parameter \(w\) und \(b\) unabhängig voneinander auf den Fehler auswirken, betrachten wir sie einzeln:
Linker Plot: Zeigt den MSE-Verlauf in Abhängigkeit von einem Parameter (\(w\) oder \(b\)), während der andere fixiert bleibt.
Rechter Plot: Zeigt die zugehörige partielle Ableitung \(\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial w}\) bzw. \(\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial b}\).
Wir führen Gradient Descent Updates nur für einen Parameter durch, nach der Update-Regel:
\(\text{Parameter}_{\text{neu}} = \text{Parameter}_{\text{alt}} - \alpha \cdot \frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \text{Parameter}}\)
wobei \(\alpha\) die Lernrate ist.
Der Gradient zeigt in die Richtung des steilsten Anstiegs, deshalb das - Vorzeichen, weil wir in Richtung des steilsten Abstiegs updaten.


Code
# ∂MSE/∂w bei fixem b
# entkopplung von w und b sichtbar durch zentrieren

def viz_pderivate(term: Calculator, axis, fixed_param_value, label_x_axis):
  lab = input_check(label_x_axis)
  if lab == "w":
    mse = term.mse(axis, fixed_param_value * np.ones_like(axis))
    grad_component = term.grad_w(axis,fixed_param_value)
    title_ = "b"
  else:
    mse = term.mse(fixed_param_value * np.ones_like(axis), axis)
    grad_component = term.grad_b(fixed_param_value,axis)
    title_ = "w"

  fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14,4), constrained_layout=True)
  axL.plot(axis, mse, alpha=0.6)
  axL.set_xlabel(lab)
  axL.set_title(f"MSE with fixed ({title_}={fixed_param_value})")
  axL.set_ylabel("MSE")
  axR.plot(axis, grad_component)
  axR.axhline(0, ls="--", lw=1)
  axR.set_xlabel(lab)
  axR.set_ylabel(f"∂MSE/∂{lab}")
  axR.set_title(f"∂MSE/∂{lab}")
  return fig, (axL,axR), fixed_param_value

def viz_update(term: Calculator,
               ax,
               ax2,
               update_trgt,
               fixed_param_value,
               label_x_axis,
               learning_rate = 0.01,
               n_loop=1
               ):

  lab = input_check(label_x_axis)
  x , y, grad_list, step = [], [], [], []
  counter = 0

  for i in range(n_loop):

    if lab == "w":
      mse = term.mse(update_trgt, fixed_param_value)
      grad_component = term.grad_w(update_trgt,fixed_param_value)
    else:
      mse = term.mse(fixed_param_value, update_trgt)
      grad_component = term.grad_b(fixed_param_value,update_trgt)

    x.append(update_trgt)
    y.append(mse)
    grad_list.append(grad_component)

    #plot the start point
    ax.plot(update_trgt, mse, "go", ms=3)

    updadte_step = - (learning_rate * grad_component)
    step.append(updadte_step)

    update_trgt += updadte_step

2.7 7. Limitationen der globalen Lernrate und der vereinfachten update Regel
Aus den obigen Plots wird deutlich: Eine einzige, globale Lernrate \(\alpha\) für alle Parameter ist selbst in diesem stark vereinfachten Szenario problematisch.

2.7.0.1 Was wir hier stark vereinfacht haben ( die wichtigsten Punkte):
1. Dimensionalität: Nur 2 Modell Parameter statt Tausende bis Millionen
2. Stochastizität: Vollständiger Gradient auf allen Daten, kein Mini-Batch Rauschen
3. Nicht-Konvexität: Einfache konvexe Loss-Funktion mit einem globalen Minimum - Reale tiefe neuronale Netze sind Hochgradig nicht-konvex - Unzählige lokale Minima - Sattelpunkte (Gradient = 0, aber kein Minimum) - Flache Plateaus (winzige Gradienten, kaum Fortschritt) - Schmale “Täler” und steile “Klippen” - Ill-conditioned Loss-Landschaften - Eine feste LR kann in flachen Regionen stecken bleiben oder in steilen Regionen “überschießen”
4. Keine Vanishing/Exploding Gradients
5. Keine Parameter-Abhängigkeiten: \(w\) und \(b\) unabhängig betrachtet
Trotz dieser Vereinfachungen sehen wir bereits in unserem simplen 2D-Fall: - Unterschiedliche Parameter haben unterschiedliche Gradienten-Skalen - Eine Lernrate, die für \(w\) gut funktioniert, kann für \(b\) suboptimal sein - Die optimale Lernrate ändert sich während des Trainings (groß am Anfang, kleiner am Ende)

2.9 9. Training
We train the model for 400 epochs. The core idea is:

Create a prediction using the current parameters.
Compute the training loss by comparing the prediction with the true values from the training set.
Compute the two components of the gradient.
Update \(w\) and \(b\) using a learning rate \(\alpha = 0.01\).
Validate the model on the validation set using the updated parameters.

train_loss, val_loss , pred_history = [], [], []
w_path, b_path = [], []

def train_step(x_train,y_train,w,b):
  y_hat = predict(x_train,w,b)
  mg = m_grad(x_train,y_train,y_hat)
  bg = b_grad(y_train,y_hat)
  w = update_target(w,mg)
  b = update_target(b,bg)
  y_hat_updated = predict(x_train,w,b)
  loss = mse(y_train,y_hat_updated)
  pred_history.append(y_hat_updated)
  w_path.append(w)
  b_path.append(b)
  return w,b,loss

def validate(x_val,y_val,w,b):
  y_hat_val = predict(x_val, w, b)
  v_loss = mse(y_val, y_hat_val)
  return v_loss


for e in range(1,epoch+1):

  v_loss = validate(x_val,y_val,w,b)
  train_loss.append(t_loss)
  val_loss.append(v_loss)

2.11 11. Viszualize Gradient Norm
Der Gradient ist ein Vektor, der an jedem Punkt \((w, b)\) in die Richtung des steilsten Anstiegs zeigt. In unserem Fall hat er zwei Komponenten: die partielle Ableitung nach \(w\) und nach \(b\). Diese Struktur macht eine direkte Visualisierung in 3D schwierig, wir müssten an jedem Punkt zwei separate Pfeile oder einen Vektorpfeil zeigen, was schnell unübersichtlich wird. Natürlich gibt es auch Möglichkeiten Losslandscapes in n-dimensionalen Parameterräumen vereinfacht darzustellen, aber das würde den Rahmen unseres Themas hier sprengen.
Stattdessen visualisieren wir die Gradient Norm, also die Länge des Gradienten-Vektors:
\[\|\nabla \text{MSE}\| = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial w}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial b}\right)^2}\]
Die Norm ist ein einzelner Skalar-Wert, der uns wichtige Informationen liefert: Sie misst, wie stark sich die Loss-Funktion an dieser Stelle verändert, unabhängig von der konkreten Richtung. Eine große Norm bedeutet, dass wir uns in einer steilen Region befinden, egal ob die Steigung von \(w\), von \(b\), oder von beiden kommt. Eine kleine Norm hingegen signalisiert eine flache Region, und im Minimum, Maximum sowie an Sattelpunkten wird die Norm zu Null.
Die Gradient Norm bestimmt direkt die Schrittgröße beim Gradient Descent Update: In Regionen mit großer Norm (steile Hänge) macht dieser vereinfachte Algorithmus große Schritte, während er in flachen Regionen nur kleine Schritte macht. Das sehen wir aus der Visualisierung.

text:
2.13 13. Lineares Modell und Designmatrix
Wir betrachten ein lineares Regressionsmodell. Linear in diesem Kontext bedeutet für uns nicht eine Gerade, sondern bezieht sich auf den Parameterraum \(w\). Der Featureraum \(X\) kann nichtlinear sein, beispielsweise \([1,\; x,\; x^2]\).
Da wir in unserem Fall eine lineare Gleichung approximieren wollen, mit
\[f(x) = m \cdot x + b,\]
bewegen wir uns in einem zweidimensionalen Parameterraum → \(w_1 \cdot x + w_0 \cdot 1\).
Natürlich könnte man diesen erweitern, jedoch muss eine Semantik dahinterstecken. Beispielsweise wäre
\[w_2 \cdot x_1 + w_1 \cdot x_1 + w_0 \cdot 1\]
nichts anderes als
\[(w_2 + w_1) \cdot x_1 + w_0 \cdot 1.\]
Das ist problematisch, da wir nun in der Designmatrix eine lineare Abhängigkeit geschaffen haben. Dadurch ist \(\Phi^\top \Phi\) nicht mehr garantiert invertierbar, weil
\[\operatorname{rank}(\Phi) < D+1.\]
Das Gleichungssystem hätte dann unendlich viele Lösungen, und die folgende Gleichung könnte nicht mehr verwendet werden und wir müssten einen anderen Ansatz wählen.
Es gibt Wege, wie man den Feature-Raum über Feature-Engineering sinnvoll erweitern kann. Das werden wir uns jedoch in einem späteren Kapitel anschauen.
\[
\hat{y} = f(x; w) = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_D x_D = w^T \phi(x)
\]
mit
\[
\phi(x) =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\
x_1 \\
\vdots \\
x_D
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
w =
\begin{pmatrix}
w_0 \\
w_1 \\
\vdots \\
w_D
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Für \(n\) Datenpunkte fassen wir alle Feature-Vektoren zu einer Designmatrix \(\Phi\) zusammen:
\[
\Phi =
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_1)^T \\
\phi(x_2)^T \\
\vdots \\
\phi(x_n)^T
\end{pmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (D+1)}
\]
Dann gilt kompakt
\[
\hat{y} = \Phi w
\]

text:
2.14 14. Fehlerfunktion (SSE/MSE) und Normalengleichungen
Wir definieren die Summe der Fehlerquadrate (SSE) als
\[
O(w) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - w^T \phi(x_i))^2
     = \| y - \Phi w \|^2
     = (y - \Phi w)^T (y - \Phi w)
\]
Wie wir unschwer ekennen ist der MSE, nicht anderes als eine skalierung des SSE um 1/n. Da sich dadurch das Minimum nicht verändert, können wir uns die Lossoberfläche im oberen Abschnitt anschauen. Dort wird deutlich, dass mit der Konvexität, die wichtigste Eigenschaft der Loss Funktion für den Ansatz erfüllt ist.
\[
\tilde{O}(w) = \frac{1}{2} \| y - \Phi w \|^2
\]
Die Ableitung nach \(w\) ergibt:
\[
\nabla_w \tilde{O}(w)
= \Phi^T \Phi w - \Phi^T y
\]
Minimum: setze \(\nabla_w \tilde{O}(w) = 0\):
\[
\Phi^T \Phi w = \Phi^T y
\]
Das sind die Normalengleichungen. Falls \(\Phi^T \Phi\) invertierbar ist:
\[
\hat{w} = (\Phi^T \Phi)^{-1} \Phi^T y
\]

Um das zu verstehen, brauchen wir erstmal eine kleine visuelle Einordung der Timelapse und der Modellparameter. Was wir sehen ist immer ein Snapshot des Modellzustandes zum Ende einer Epoche. Also der Zustand der nach dem Update des letzen sampels zustande gekommen ist, hier Feauture -> (1,1).
Die konstante updaterate von 1 impliziert das jedes Trainingsample für das darauf folgende Sample ein update ausgelöst hat, also ein delta != 0. Die Gewichte haben sich somit unweigerlich verändert, nur wurde wurde es wieder überschrieben, da das delta dauernd zwischen -1 und 1 schwingt. Das wird aus der update Regel auch deutlich, welche auch auf den Bias übertragen werden kann. \[

1.2 The perceptron as a model
The perceptron processes inputs in three consecutive steps:

1.2.1 1. Input
The model receives an input vector x, we call this the feature vector.


1.2.2 2. Calculation
The input is linearly transformed using the weights w and the bias parameter b. We call the weighted sum z:
\[z = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b\]


1.2.3 3. Output
We pass the weighted sum z to a non-linear activation function, which in the Rosenblatt perceptron is classically the step function. In the perceptron, we call the result of this the prediction of the model:
\[\hat{y} = \text{step}(z) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } z \geq 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]


1.2.4 Complete data flow
The entire process can be represented as follows:
\[\mathbf{x} \longrightarrow \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b \longrightarrow \text{step}(z) \longrightarrow \hat{y}\]

1.3 Implementing the perceptron class
Now we will implement the perceptron as a class. We have already examined the architecture, so now we will focus on the learning rule.

1.3.1 Classic perceptron learning rule
The perceptron learns by adjusting its weights only when it makes a mistake.
For each training example, the prediction \(\hat{y}\) is compared with the true label \(y\).
This results in an error term:
\[
\delta = y - \hat{y}
\]

If \(\delta = 0\):
The prediction is correct → no adjustment.
If \(\delta = 1\):
The perceptron predicted \(0\) although \(1\) would be correct →
The weights should be shifted in the direction of \(\mathbf{x}\).
If \(\delta = -1\):
The perceptron predicted \(1\) although \(0\) would be correct →
The weights should be shifted away from \(\mathbf{x}\).

The classical perceptron learning rule is:
\[
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta \, \delta \, \mathbf{x}
\]
\[
b \leftarrow b + \eta \, \delta
\]
where \(\eta\) is the learning rate.

1.3.1.1 Intuition

Incorrectly classified positive examples (\(y = 1\)) ‘pull’ the weight vector in their direction.
Incorrectly classified negative examples (\(y = 0\)) ‘push’ the weight vector away from themselves.
Correctly classified examples have no influence on the weights.

In this way, the perceptron shifts its decision boundary until all training points (if linearly separable) are correctly classified.



Code
class Perzeptron:
    def __init__(self, input_size, activation_function):

        self.weight = rng.normal(size=(input_size,1))
        self.bias = 0.
        self.activation = activation_function

    def forward(self, X):
        """
        Berechnet die Ausgabe des Perzeptrons für ein Feauture X.

        Args:
            X: Eingabedaten, Shape (n_samples, n_features)
        Returns:
            Ausgabe des Perzeptrons nach Aktiverung, Shape (n_samples, 1)
        """
        z = X @ self.weight + self.bias
        a = self.activation(z)
        return a

    def train(self, X, y , lr=0.1, epochs=1000, error_prints=True):
        """
        Trains the perceptron using the perceptron (error-count) learning rule.

        Args:
            X (np.ndarray): Input data of shape (n_samples, n_features).
            y (np.ndarray): Target labels of shape (n_samples, 1) 
            lr (float): Learning rate
            epochs (int): Maximum number of training epochs.
            error_prints (bool) : Printing error rates -> set False for timelapse

        Returns:
            list[float]: List of error_rate per epoch
            list[float]: List of update_rate per epoch
        """
    
        error_history, update_history = [], []

        for epoch in range(epochs):
            fehler_count = 0
            for xi, yi in zip(X,y):
                xi = np.reshape(xi, (1,-1)) # (1, n_features)
                yi = np.reshape(yi, (-1,1)) # (1, 1) 
                #Forward pass 
                y_hat = self.forward(xi)

                #Calc delta
                delta = (yi - y_hat)
                delta = np.squeeze(delta)
                delta = float(delta)

                #Update weights and bias
                if delta != 0:
                    self.weight += lr * delta * xi.T
                    self.bias += lr * delta
                    fehler_count += 1

            update_rate = fehler_count/len(y)
            y_hat = self.forward(X)
            error_rate = float(np.mean(y != y_hat))
            error_history.append(error_rate)            
            update_history.append(update_rate)

            if error_prints:
                if epoch % 10 == 0:
                    print(f'Epoch {epoch}: Error Rate = {error_rate:.4f}')

            if error_rate == 0:
                print(f"Solution in Epoch {epoch}")
                return error_history, update_history
                
        return error_history, update_history

text:
1.9 Evaluation
At first glance, it is clear that the model does not converge to the minimum possible error rate of 0.25 (one misclassification). The simple reason for this is that we are not solving an optimisation problem with the perceptron. The implemented learning rule essentially states: continue training until you can separate the classes or the maximum number of epochs has been reached.
This explains the behaviour of the error rate, but not why the decision boundary no longer changes after the 20th epoch.
To understand this, we first need a little visual classification of the timelapse and the model parameters. What we see is always a snapshot of the model state at the end of an epoch. In other words, the state that resulted after the last sample was updated, in this case Feature -> (1,1).
The constant update rate of 1 implies that each training sample triggered an update for the following sample, i.e. a delta != 0. The weights have therefore inevitably changed, but they have been overwritten again because the delta constantly fluctuates between -1 and 1. This is also clear from the update rule, which can also be applied to the bias. \[
\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta \, \delta \, \mathbf{x}
\]

1.10 Outlook
In the next chapter, we will continue with the logistic perceptron, using the sigmoid activation function defined above. This will introduce two fundamental changes to our model that will simplify the path to the multi-layer perceptron. We will start by solving an optimization problem. In addition, the principle of uncertainty will be introduced. The output of the Rosenblatt perceptron is binary and does not contain any information about how certain the model is. In contrast, the logistic model with sigmoid provides a continuous output in (0,1), which can be interpreted as probability and thus provides a measure of uncertainty. In the figurative context with regard to uncertainty, this means that the perceptron is always 100% certain in its prediction, even if it is wrong.

text:
2.5 5. Loss Function
We can see straight away that our randomly initialized function does not represent the data well. To quantify this, we need a loss function.
For the regression problem we wish to solve, we’ll keep it simple by using the mean squared error (MSE). In the summation notation below, our linear model contains a coupling term \(2 \cdot b \cdot w \cdot \sum(x)\). By centering \(x\), the sum becomes 0 and the term is therefore later eliminated.
In this simplified setting, the model has only one input feature. Therefore, the weight \(w\) and the bias \(b\) can also be interpreted as the slope and intercept of a linear function.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\displaystyle
MSE &= \frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} error_i^2 \\[8pt]
    &= \frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2 \\[8pt]
    &= \frac{1}{n} \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} (b + w x_i - y_i)^2 \\[8pt]
    &= \frac{1}{n} \Bigg(
        \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} y_i^2
        - 2b \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} y_i
        - 2w \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i y_i
        + b^2 n
        + {\color{red}{2bw \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i}}
        + w^2 \sum\limits_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2
      \Bigg)
\end{aligned}
\]
Next, we put the prediction error over the training dataset into our loss function. Here, we define the error as
\[
\text{error} = \hat{y} - y
\]
where \(\hat{y}\) denotes the model prediction and \(y\) denotes the observed target value.


Code
def mse(y: np.ndarray, y_hat: np.ndarray):
  return (1/len(y)) * np.sum((y_hat-y)**2)

def dmse_dyhat(y: np.ndarray, y_hat: np.ndarray):
  return (2/y.size) * (y_hat-y)

Looking at the formula, we can already see that large errors have a stronger influence on the MSE because the error term is squared. Plotting the function makes this relationship even more intuitive.
A common misconception is that we can simply explore a dataset, identify outliers, and remove them. In practice, this can quickly lead to wrong assumptions.
This becomes especially clear in biology or medicine. The same blood sample sent to different laboratories can lead to different measured values. These differences may arise from different measurement procedures, insufficient cooling during transport, or intrinsic biological reactions.
A model should therefore be able to handle a certain amount of noise. This does not mean that obvious measurement errors should never be corrected. However, deciding whether a value is noise, a true rare observation, or a measurement error often requires domain knowledge.
Attentive readers may already think about methods such as scaling, transformations, normalization, or more robust loss functions to reduce the influence of large errors. We will revisit these ideas in later chapters.
The second plot shows the derivative of the squared error. While the MSE itself grows quadratically, its derivative grows linearly with the error.
This gives us an important intuition for Gradient Descent. Large errors do not only produce a large loss, they also produce a larger derivative. As a result, these errors can have a strong influence on the optimization process.

class Calculator():
  def __init__(self, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, start_axis=0, stop_axis=4):
    try:
      assert x.size == y.size, "Shape missmatch, can cause Problems later"
    except AssertionError as error:
      print(error)
    # Feauture and Target
    self.x = x
    self.y = y
    #Terms from MSE Formula
    self.Syy = np.sum(y**2)
    self.Sxy = np.sum(y * x)
    self.Sxx = np.sum(x**2)
    self.Sx = np.sum(x)
    self.Sy = np.sum(y)
    self.n = len(y)

    #axis
    self.w_axis : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.b_axis : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.w_mesh : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.b_mesh : np.ndarray | None = None
    self.set_mesh(start_axis,stop_axis)

  def mse(self, w = None, b = None, is_mesh=False):
    """
     Compute the MSE for given values of w and b.
     if parameters are a mesh grid:
      is mesh -> true
    """ 
    if w is not None and b is not None:
      w = np.asarray(w)
      b = np.asarray(b)
    elif (w is None) != (b is None):
      raise ValueError("w or b value missing")
    else:
      if not is_mesh:
          w = self.w_axis
          b = self.b_axis
      else:
        w = self.w_mesh
        b = self.b_mesh

    term = (self.Syy - 2*w*self.Sxy - 2*b*self.Sy + w**2 * self.Sxx
            + 2*w*b*self.Sx + self.n*(b**2) )
    mse = term/self.n
    return mse


  def grad_b(self, w, b):
    term = (- 2*self.Sy
            + 2*w*self.Sx + 2*self.n*(b))
    dmse_db = term/self.n
    return dmse_db

  def grad_w(self, w, b):
    term = (- 2*self.Sxy + 2 * w * self.Sxx
            + 2*b*self.Sx )
    dmse_dw = term/self.n
    return dmse_dw

  def set_mesh(self, axis_start: float, axis_stop: float, n=1):
    if n == 1:
      n = self.n
    self.w_axis = np.linspace(axis_start, axis_stop, n)
    self.b_axis = np.linspace(axis_start, axis_stop, n)
    self.w_mesh, self.b_mesh = np.meshgrid(self.w_axis,self.b_axis)

text:
2.6 6. Partial Derivatives and Gradient Descent in 1D
To understand how the parameters \(w\) and \(b\) affect the loss, we first examine them one at a time by fixing one parameter and varying the other.
Left plot: Shows the MSE as a function of one parameter, either \(w\) or \(b\), while the other parameter is held fixed.
Right plot: Shows the corresponding partial derivative, either \(\frac{\partial \mathrm{MSE}}{\partial w}\) or \(\frac{\partial \mathrm{MSE}}{\partial b}\).
We then perform Gradient Descent updates for only one parameter at a time. The update rule for a parameter is
\[
\mathrm{Parameter}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\mathrm{Parameter}_{\mathrm{old}}
-
\alpha \cdot
\frac{\partial \mathrm{MSE}}{\partial \mathrm{Parameter}}
\]
Here, \(\alpha\) is the learning rate.
The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase. Since we want to minimize the loss, we update in the opposite direction. This is why the update rule contains a minus sign.


Code
# Decoupling of W and B by centring x at the begin

def viz_pderivate(term: Calculator, axis, fixed_param_value: float, label_x_axis):
  """
  Plot MSE slice and the corresponding partial derivative.

  If label_x_axis is "w", the function varies w and keeps b fixed vice versa.
  """
  lab = input_check(label_x_axis)
  if lab == "w":
    mse = term.mse(axis, fixed_param_value * np.ones_like(axis))
    grad_component = term.grad_w(axis,fixed_param_value)
    title_ = "b"
  else:
    mse = term.mse(fixed_param_value * np.ones_like(axis), axis)
    grad_component = term.grad_b(fixed_param_value,axis)
    title_ = "w"

  fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14,4), constrained_layout=True)
  axL.plot(axis, mse, alpha=0.6)
  axL.set_xlabel(lab)
  axL.set_title(f"MSE with fixed ({title_}={fixed_param_value})")
  axL.set_ylabel("MSE")
  axR.plot(axis, grad_component)
  axR.axhline(0, ls="--", lw=1)
  axR.set_xlabel(lab)
  axR.set_ylabel(f"∂MSE/∂{lab}")
  axR.set_title(f"∂MSE/∂{lab}")
  return fig, (axL,axR), fixed_param_value

def viz_update(term: Calculator,
               ax,
               ax2,
               update_trgt,
               fixed_param_value,
               label_x_axis,
               learning_rate = 0.01,
               n_loop=1
               ):

  lab = input_check(label_x_axis)
  x , y, grad_list, step = [], [], [], []
  counter = 0

  for i in range(n_loop):

    if lab == "w":
      mse = term.mse(update_trgt, fixed_param_value)
      grad_component = term.grad_w(update_trgt,fixed_param_value)
    else:
      mse = term.mse(fixed_param_value, update_trgt)
      grad_component = term.grad_b(fixed_param_value,update_trgt)

    x.append(update_trgt)
    y.append(mse)
    grad_list.append(grad_component)

    #plot the start point
    ax.plot(update_trgt, mse, "go", ms=3)

    updadte_step = - (learning_rate * grad_component)
    step.append(updadte_step)

    update_trgt += updadte_step

    #print(f"mse = {y[i]} , grad = {grad_list[i]} , w = {x[i]}")
    if counter >= 1:
      ax.arrow(x[i-1], y[i-1], step[i-1], y[i] - y[i-1], color="red", width=0.02, head_width=0.1,head_length=0.10,)


    counter += 1
  ax2.scatter(x,grad_list, c="red", s=15)

section: 2.7 7. Limitations of a Global Learning Rate and the Simplified Update Rule
text:
2.7 7. Limitations of a Global Learning Rate and the Simplified Update Rule
The plots above reveal an important limitation: even in this highly simplified setting, using one single global learning rate \(\alpha\) for all parameters can be challenging.
A learning rate that works well for one parameter may be too small or too large for another parameter, especially when the parameters influence the loss on different scales.

2.7.0.1 What we strongly simplified here (the most important points):
1. Dimensionality: Only 2 model parameters instead of thousands to billions
2. Stochasticity: Full gradient computed on all data, no mini-batch noise
3. Non-convexity: Simple convex loss function with one global minimum

Deep neural networks are highly non-convex

countless local minima
Saddle points, where the gradient is zero but not a minimum
Flat plateaus with tiny gradients and little progress
Narrow valleys and steep cliffs
Ill-conditioned loss landscapes

A fixed learning rate can get stuck in flat regions or overshoot in steep regions

4. No vanishing or exploding gradients
5. No parameter dependencies: \(w\) and \(b\) are considered separately
Despite these simplifications, we can already observe in our simple 2D case:

Different parameters can have different gradient scales
A learning rate that works well for \(w\) can be suboptimal for \(b\)
The optimal learning rate can change during training

Outlook:
Do not worry if some of these terms are unfamiliar at this point. We will examine them more closely throughout the course. For now, the goal is to build intuition. In the next notebook, we will move from Gradient Descent to Stochastic Gradient Descent and other optimizers, and we will also look at strategies for adapting the learning rate.


2.7.1 Different Learning Rates
We now examine how the optimization process changes when we increase the learning rate \(\alpha\).

2.10 10. Visualizing the Loss
In the next step, we visualize the training and validation loss. Even for such a simple problem, this gives us useful information about the training process.
We can see that the model initially converges quickly toward the optimum. After that, the curve visibly flattens, because the gradients become very small near the minimum and further improvements happen only slowly, this interpretation is specific to our simple two-parameter MSE example.
The almost identical behavior of the training and validation loss suggests that the model generalizes well to the validation data. The remaining error is therefore not mainly caused by insufficient training. Instead, it is largely due to irreducible noise in the data. In more complex scenarios, structural limitations of the model class could also contribute to such a remaining error.
Training for more epochs would therefore not meaningfully reduce the loss any further.

2.10.0.1 Note
When training deep neural networks, computational cost can grow quickly, so long training runs can become expensive. For a synthetically generated dataset like the one in our example, this is not a major issue. In real-world scenarios, however, it often matters.
A common strategy for reducing unnecessary training time is Early Stopping. If the validation loss does not improve by more than a predefined threshold for several consecutive epochs, training is stopped automatically. This saves computation time and avoids optimization steps that no longer improve generalization.
The effect of Early Stopping on certain training dynamics, such as Grokking, will be discussed separately later.

text:
2.11 11. Visualizing the Gradient Norm
The gradient is a vector that points in the direction of steepest increase at each point \((w, b)\). In our case, it has two components: the partial derivative with respect to \(w\) and the partial derivative with respect to \(b\).
This structure makes direct 3D visualisation difficult. We would have to show two separate arrows or a vector arrow at each point, which would quickly become confusing. Of course, there are also ways to represent loss landscapes in simplified form within n-dimensional parameter spaces, but that would go beyond the scope of our discussion here.
Instead, we visualize the gradient norm, which is the length of the gradient vector:
\[
\left\lVert \nabla \mathrm{MSE} \right\rVert
=
\sqrt{
\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{MSE}}{\partial w}\right)^2
+
\left(\frac{\partial \mathrm{MSE}}{\partial b}\right)^2
}
\]
The norm is a single scalar value that provides us with important information. It measures how much the loss function changes at this point, regardless of the specific direction. A large norm indicates that we are in a steep region, regardless of whether the slope comes from \(w\), from \(b\), or from both. A small norm, on the other hand, indicates a flat region, and at minima, maxima and saddle points, the norm becomes zero.
The gradient norm directly determines the step size in the gradient descent update in combination with the learning rate. In regions with a large norm (steep slopes), this simplified algorithm takes large steps, whilst in flat regions it takes only small steps. We can see this from the visualisation.

In these visualizations, we plot the individual gradient components \(\frac{\partial MSE}{\partial w}\) and \(\frac{\partial MSE}{\partial b}\). The height of each surface therefore does not represent the loss itself, but only the value of the corresponding partial derivative at each point in the parameter space.
Each surface shows how strongly the loss changes with respect to one parameter while considering the current position in the \((w, b)\) parameter space.
A positive value means that increasing the corresponding parameter would locally increase the loss. A negative value means that increasing the corresponding parameter would locally decrease the loss. Values close to zero indicate that the loss changes only weakly in that parameter direction.

This intuition will be important later when we train neural networks. The main idea remains the same: compute predictions, measure the loss, compute gradients, and update the parameters. In neural networks, however, we will additionally deal with activation functions, multiple layers, and many more parameters.
Since the model in this notebook is only a simple linear model, there is also an analytical solution. Instead of finding the parameters iteratively with Gradient Descent, we can compute the optimal linear regression parameters directly using the method of least squares.

title: 2  Introduction to Gradient Descent
text:
2.13 13. Linear Model and Design Matrix
We consider a linear regression model. Linear in this context does not mean a straight line for us, but refers to the parameter space \(w\). The feature space \(X\) can be nonlinear, for example \([1, x, x^2]\).
Since in our case we want to approximate a linear equation,
\[
f(x) = m \cdot x + b,
\]
we move in a two-dimensional parameter space:
\[
w_1 \cdot x + w_0 \cdot 1.
\]
Of course, we could extend this parameter space, but there has to be meaningful semantics behind it. For example,
\[
w_2 \cdot x_1 + w_1 \cdot x_1 + w_0 \cdot 1
\]
is nothing more than
\[
(w_2 + w_1) \cdot x_1 + w_0 \cdot 1.
\]
This is problematic because we have now created a linear dependency in the design matrix. As a result, \(\Phi^\top \Phi\) is no longer guaranteed to be invertible, because
\[
\operatorname{rank}(\Phi) < D+1.
\]
The system of equations would then have infinitely many solutions, and the following inverse-based equation could no longer be used directly. We would have to choose another approach.
There are ways to extend the feature space in a meaningful way through feature engineering. However, we will look at this in a later chapter.
\[
\hat{y} = f(x; w) = w_0 + w_1 x_1 + \dots + w_D x_D = w^\top \phi(x)
\]
with
\[
\phi(x) =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 \\
x_1 \\
\vdots \\
x_D
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
w =
\begin{pmatrix}
w_0 \\
w_1 \\
\vdots \\
w_D
\end{pmatrix}
\]
For \(n\) data points, we combine all feature vectors into a design matrix \(\Phi\):
\[
\Phi =
\begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_1)^T \\
\phi(x_2)^T \\
\vdots \\
\phi(x_n)^T
\end{pmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (D+1)}
\]
Then we can write compactly:
\[
\hat{y} = \Phi w
\]

title: 2  Introduction to Gradient Descent
text:
2.14 14. Error Function (SSE/MSE) and Normal Equations
We define the sum of squared errors (SSE) as
\[
O(w) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - w^\top \phi(x_i))^2
= | y - \Phi w |^2
= (y - \Phi w)^\top (y - \Phi w)
\]
As we can easily see, the MSE is nothing more than a scaled version of the SSE by a factor of \(\frac{1}{n}\). Since this scaling does not change the location of the minimum, we can refer back to the loss surface from the previous section. There, we can see that the loss function is convex, which is the key property that makes the following analytical approach possible.
\[
\tilde{O}(w) = \frac{1}{2} | y - \Phi w |^2.
\]
The factor \(\frac{1}{2}\) does not change the minimum. It only simplifies the derivative.
Taking the derivative with respect to \(w\) gives
\[
\nabla_w \tilde{O}(w)
= \Phi^\top \Phi w - \Phi^\top y.
\]
At the minimum, we set the gradient equal to zero:
\[
\nabla_w \tilde{O}(w) = 0.
\]
This gives
\[
\Phi^\top \Phi w = \Phi^\top y.
\]
